# Ways of writing linear maps

We saw in the previous chapter that, once we choose a basis for a vector space $V$, we can write vectors as their list of coefficients relative to this basis.

Suppose we have a linear function $L : V \to W$.
How can we write this in a basis?

## Maps in finite dimensions

Let's consider the linear function $F : P_2 \to \mathbb R^2$ given by
$$
F(x^2) = (0,0) ,\quad F(x) = (1,0) ,\quad F(1) = (0,1).
$$
Let's express this in a basis.
Consider the basis $[x^2,x,1]$ for $P_2$ and $[(1,0),(0,1)]$ for $\mathbb R^2$.

Then the vector $x \in P_2$ corresponds to the list of coefficients 
$$
\left[  \begin{aligned} 0 \\ 1 \\ 0 \end{aligned}\right]
$$
and the vector $(1,0) \in \mathbb R^2$ corresponds to the list of coefficients
$$
\left[  \begin{aligned} 1 \\ 0 \end{aligned}\right].
$$

So, whatever our expression for $F$ is in coordinates, it must fit in
$$
F \left( \left[  \begin{aligned} 0 \\ 1 \\ 0 \end{aligned}\right] \right) = \left[  \begin{aligned} 1 \\ 0 \end{aligned}\right],
$$
and similarly,
$$
F \left( \left[  \begin{aligned} 0 \\ 0 \\ 1 \end{aligned}\right] \right) = \left[  \begin{aligned} 0 \\ 1 \end{aligned}\right], \quad 
F \left( \left[  \begin{aligned} 1 \\ 0 \\ 0 \end{aligned}\right] \right) = \left[  \begin{aligned} 0 \\ 0 \end{aligned}\right].
$$

First, let's note that, when we're applying a linear function to the coefficients of a vector written as a column, we usually don't write the parentheses after the function name.
That is, we will write function applications like
$$
F \left[  \begin{aligned} 1 \\ 0 \\ 0 \end{aligned}\right] = \left[  \begin{aligned} 0 \\ 0 \end{aligned}\right], \quad 
F \left[  \begin{aligned} 0 \\ 1 \\ 0 \end{aligned}\right] = \left[  \begin{aligned} 1 \\ 0 \end{aligned}\right], \quad 
F \left[  \begin{aligned} 0 \\ 0 \\ 1 \end{aligned}\right] = \left[  \begin{aligned} 0 \\ 1 \end{aligned}\right].
$$

### Writing linear functions as 2-dimensional arrays.

We will introduce the notation for writing $F$ above in coordinates.
Then we will develop fast processes for computing function application, composition, sums, multiples, and inverses of linear functions all while remaining "in coordinates".

The motivation will be the following:

If we know a linear function on a basis for its domain, we know it everywhere.
In particular,

$$
\begin{aligned}
F \left[  \begin{aligned} a \\ b \\ c \end{aligned}\right] 
=& F \left( a  \left[  \begin{aligned} 1 \\ 0 \\ 0 \end{aligned}\right] + b \left[  \begin{aligned} 0 \\ 1 \\ 0 \end{aligned}\right] + c \left[  \begin{aligned} 0 \\ 0 \\ 1 \end{aligned}\right]\right) \\
=& a F \left[  \begin{aligned} 1 \\ 0 \\ 0 \end{aligned}\right] + b F \left[  \begin{aligned} 0 \\ 1 \\ 0 \end{aligned}\right] + c F \left[  \begin{aligned} 0 \\ 0 \\ 1 \end{aligned}\right] \\
=& a \left[  \begin{aligned} 0 \\ 0 \end{aligned}\right] + b \left[  \begin{aligned} 1 \\ 0 \end{aligned}\right] + c \left[  \begin{aligned} 0 \\ 1 \end{aligned}\right]\\
=& \left[  \begin{aligned} (0)a + (1)b + (0)c \\ (0)a + (0)b + (1)c \end{aligned}\right] .
\end{aligned}
$$

The way we will write $F$ in coordinates, is to write it as a 2-dimensional array of numbers.
$$
\begin{bmatrix}
\_ & \_ & \_\\
\_ & \_ & \_
\end{bmatrix}.
$$

The number of columns of the array is the dimension of the **domain** of $F$, so in this case there are three columns.
The number of rows of the array is the dimension of the **codomain** of $F$, so in this case there are two rows.

The first column of the array is where $F$ sends the first basis vector of its domain.
If we use the basis we have already chosen, then the array for $F$ looks like
$$
\begin{bmatrix}
0 & \_ & \_\\
0 & \_ & \_
\end{bmatrix}
$$
because $F$ takes its first basis vector to $(0,0)$, which, in the coordinates for the codomain, is the column 

$$
\begin{bmatrix}
0 \\
0 
\end{bmatrix}.
$$

Similarly, the second column of the array is where $F$ sends the second basis vector
$$
\begin{bmatrix}
0 & 1 & \_\\
0 & 0 & \_
\end{bmatrix}
$$
and the third column is where $F$ sends the third basis vector
$$
\begin{bmatrix}
0 & 1 & 0\\
0 & 0 & 1
\end{bmatrix}.
$$

This two dimensional array of numbers we used to represent $F$ is called a *matrix*.

::: {#exr-write-as-matrix}
> Consider the linear function $G: P_2 \to \mathbb R^2$ given by
> $$
> G(x^2) = (2,0) ,\quad G(x) = (-1,3) ,\quad G(1) = (7,\pi) .
> $$
> 
> Using the same basis that we used for $F$ above, write the matrix for $G$.
:::

## Maps involving infinite dimensional spaces

We know that some vector spaces do not have a finite dimension (for example, the space of continuous functions $\mathbb R \to \mathbb R$).
Since the size of a matrix for a linear map is determined by the dimension of the domain (the number of columns) and the dimension of the codomain (the number of rows), it is not possible to represent a linear function to or from an infinite dimensional vector space as a matrix.
